title: Compose eight bars on a chord pattern
summary: Play a repeating chord pattern with the left hand, then make up eight bars of tune over the top.
materials: the piece from your teacher, with a pencil

figure.alt: A row of eight boxes, standing for the eight bars of tune made up with the right hand over the repeating four-chord pattern held steady in the left hand.

steps.title: Compose eight bars on a chord pattern
steps.body:
A chord pattern is a small set of chords repeated in the same order. It is the kind of thing a left hand can play without thinking, once it is learned. Once the left hand is steady, the right hand is free to try things over the top.

1. Get a simple chord pattern from your teacher, or use one from a piece you already know: four chords, repeating.
2. Play the pattern with the left hand alone until it repeats without you having to think about it.
3. With the right hand, try a short line over the top, eight bars long, using notes that belong to the chords underneath.
4. Once you find eight bars you like, play the whole thing through and write the notes down.

Composing is just playing with more choices than usual, and a steady chord pattern is what keeps those choices from turning into chaos.

figure.alt: A one-octave keyboard from middle C. C4 and G4 are highlighted, a fifth apart, the interval the text names: a root note and the fifth above it, whose wiggle rates make a simple 3 to 2 ratio.

steps.title: Simple ratios sound sweet
steps.body:
Two notes sound settled together when their wiggle rates make a simple ratio. A fifth, like C up to G, is a ratio of 3 to 2. A fourth, like C up to F, is 4 to 3. The simpler the ratio, the more the two notes seem to agree.

Predict first: if a root note wiggles 220 times a second, how fast does the fifth above it wiggle? Write your number in the Practice log.

Measure: open a tuner app, play a note and read the number it shows, then play the fifth above it and read that number.

Compare: divide the second number by the first. Is it close to 3 to 2, which is 1.5?

Teach it: explain why a chord built from fifths sounds settled, while two notes picked at random often sound like a clash.

figure.alt: A row of eight boxes for the finished eight bars of tune, played with both hands once the chord pattern underneath is steady.

steps.title: Four sittings
steps.body: Fifteen minutes each. Tick a sitting when it is done. Days do not matter; sittings do.
checklist: Sitting 1: play the chord pattern alone until it is steady, no right hand yet
Sitting 2: try right-hand ideas over the pattern, four bars at a time
Sitting 3: settle on eight bars you like, and write the notes down
Sitting 4: play the finished eight bars with both hands, then once as if recording
An old piece played once, just for the fun of it

steps.title: Record this week's version
steps.prompt: Play the chord pattern alone once, then play your finished eight bars with both hands, hands in the frame.
